At the edge of the town, where the last houses loosened into fields, there was a bench facing west.

Nobody remembered who had put it there. Its green paint had peeled in long curls, and one leg sank slightly into the earth. Still, people sat on it: after arguments, before decisions, on evenings when the sky seemed to be doing something worth watching.

A girl came there most days with a notebook. She was trying to write a story about a person who knew exactly what to do. Every time she began, the person turned out to be someone else: a lighthouse keeper, a thief, a woman with a garden full of white flowers. None of them knew what to do. They only kept going, which was not the same thing.

One evening, an old man was already on the bench. He wore a brown coat and held a paper bag folded neatly at the top.

“Are you writing?” he asked.

“I’m trying.”

“Good,” he said. “Trying is how most things begin.”

She looked at his bag. “What’s in there?”

“Two pears. I bought three, but I ate one on the way.”

“Were they good?”

“I don’t know yet.”

He handed her one. She took it. The pear was cool and heavy in her palm.

They watched the sun lower itself behind the fields. The girl took a bite. Sweetness, then a little tartness near the skin. She wrote this down, though it wasn’t part of her story.

The old man stood and brushed dirt from his coat.

“Will you be here tomorrow?” she asked.

“Probably,” he said. “Unless I’m somewhere else.”

This seemed to her an unsatisfactory answer, but also a true one.

After he left, she opened her notebook to a clean page. She did not write about a person who knew exactly what to do. Instead, she wrote about a girl on a bench, holding half a pear, while the evening moved around her without asking permission.

The story did not solve anything. The girl in it did not become wise or fearless. But she stayed until the sky went dark, and when she finally stood, she carried the notebook home.

For a while, that was enough.

Years later, the bench was gone. The fields had become houses, then a small grocery store with bright windows. The girl—no longer a girl—sometimes passed through town and tried to remember which way the sunset fell. She could never be sure.

But in a drawer at home, she kept the old notebook. The pages had yellowed. The ink had faded. On one of them, in a hand she almost recognized, were the words: *Sweetness, then a little tartness near the skin.*

She would read them and remember that not every beginning announces itself. Some arrive as a stranger’s answer, a pear held out beneath a wide sky, or the moment you stop waiting to know what happens next.

Sometimes the story is simply that you stayed.
